keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. Area check: the page gives 'approximately 8,000 km2' for the mid-16th century (no infobox area); the Siena and Grosseto provinces come to about 7,840 km2 on the gazetteer, a ratio of 0.98. The province pair is a reading of the whole life from 1335: the page dates Massa (1335) but not Grosseto, the coastal ports or the other acquisitions, so the earlier growth is unresolved (confidence 2).

ledger.note: 1125: the Republic of Siena is founded. 'The foundation of the Republic of Siena is traditionally dated to 1125'; the extent of the first commune is my reading.

1260: Montalcino becomes a satellite of Siena. 'As a satellite of Siena since the Battle of Montaperti in 1260'; the Republic of Siena page adds that on 4 September 1260 the Sienese Ghibellines defeated the Florentine Guelphs at Montaperti. The status (outright annexation or dependence) is not on the page.

1286: the government of the Nine (Nove) takes over Siena. 'In 1286 the Nove ('the Nine') government was established to rule Siena' (the infobox says 1287; the government table 1286-1355). No change of land; colour and dossier continue.

region.text: Massa Marittima and its mining district

ledger.note: 1335: Siena subjugates Massa. Massa Marittima page: 'subsequently being subjugated by it in 1335'; the Siena page: 'with the conquest of the Republic of Massa, Siena was able to take possession of its rich mining district'. The Massa page also gives the free commune as 1255-1337.

1547: Spain holds Siena through a governor. 'From 1547 to 1552, the Spanish-installed governor of Siena was Diego Hurtado de Mendoza.' The Siena page says only that Charles V put a Spanish garrison in Siena after the chaos of the 1520s, with no year; 1547 is the governor's start.

17 July 1552: the Sienese expel the Spanish garrison and take a French one. 'Sienese rebels welcomed a French garrison to defend it against Spanish recapture attempts'; the Franco-Sienese army 'managed to expel the Spanish garrison'. Siena is then allied to France (protectorate in effect; France's dossier would carry the tint).

ledger.note: January 1554: Florence and Spain besiege Siena. The page's timeline gives the siege as 'January 1554 - 21 April 1555'; the decisive Florentine-Spanish victory at Marciano came on 2 August 1554 ('Decisive Florentine-Spanish victory over Siena and France'). The page does not map the fighting, so the zone is the whole state (my reading).

region.text: Massa Marittima, whose fortress capitulated in 1554

ledger.note: 3 February 1555: Massa Marittima is incorporated by the Medici state. 'On February 3, 1555 the city was incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Tuscany' (the page's anachronism; it was the Duchy of Florence); in 1554 'the Massa fortress capitulated, besieged by the Spaniards led by Carlo Gonzaga'.

ledger.note: 21 April 1555: Siena surrenders. 'Siena surrendered to Spain on 21 April 1555, marking the end of the Republic' (the Italian War page body says 15 April, its timeline 21 April; History of Siena says 17 April). Spain then 'ceded Siena's entire territory to the Duchy of Florence' (year not on the page; the Florence ledger has July 1557), keeping coastal fortresses that became the State of the Presidi.

notes: Written from five pages. Unsettled: how and when Siena grew from its first contado to the roughly 8,000 km2 of the 1550s (Grosseto, the coastal ports Talamone, Porto Ercole and Porto Santo Stefano, Montepulciano, Chiusi and Orbetello are undated on the pages opened); the Republic's actual extent under the Nine; the date of the Spanish garrison before 1547; the day of the surrender (15, 17 or 21 April 1555). The French garrison and alliance of 1552-1555 is a protectorate that France's dossier (or an eu-17 France batch) should carry as vassal_start with counterpart republic-of-siena; Siena's own ledger has no vassal events because the tint belongs to the suzerain. The Florence ledger (eu-13-i) records the 1555-1557 Florentine and Spanish occupation and the July 1557 grant to Cosimo; this dossier hands the land to Spain in 1555 to match. The March of Tuscany (predecessor) and the State of the Presidi (Spanish coastal fortresses) need dossiers. The Montalcino rump has its own short dossier, republic-of-siena-in-montalcino, because the Florence ledger names it as a counterpart.
